patterns.skill:
VERIFIED SCOPE ONLY: One text submission with zero dependants at revert time, in a forum the acting account owns/moderates, created and deleted by the same account via browser UI clicks. Pin = exact title (+ id from the create redirect).
Creating a Postmill submission is reverted by the submission's own native Delete button: open the created submission's permalink, click Delete in the submission article, and accept the browser confirm dialog. Pin the object by its exact title (plus the submission id from the POST /submit 302 redirect) so the delete is provably scoped to the object you created. No content capture is needed — creation-only mutation with a native inverse and no prior state to restore. Delete is permanent (Postmill has no undo/restore for submissions); child-comment cascade is NOT verified, so only use this while the submission still has zero dependants; a self-delete by the author/owner leaves no Trash or mod-log entry.
LIMITATIONS: Untested: URL and image submission types; deleting another user's submission; moderator 'remove' (Actions) vs author Delete. Untested: reverting a submission that already has comments — child-dependent deletion is untested and Trash stayed empty, so cascaded comments would be unrecoverable. Untested: title collision / pagination when locating by title (the tested forum listing was a single page). Postmill has no revision/undo for submissions; delete is permanent, no restore attempted. Browser-only access; no shell/DB verification.

VERIFIED SCOPE ONLY: One top-level comment on a submission owned by the acting account, deleted by its own author through the delete_own control. Single live example; no dependants involved.
Creation-only pattern: a comment the agent posted on a Postmill submission is undone by Postmill's own per-comment Delete (delete_own) control. No pre-state capture is required — only the created comment's identity must be recorded at creation time: the comment id read from the post-submit redirect URL (/f/<FORUM>/<SUBMISSION_ID>/-/comment/<COMMENT_ID>), with the exact body text as a fallback pin. Deletion is hard and irreversible in-app (no Trash entry, no moderation-log tombstone), so it is only valid for undoing a comment the agent itself created, and any child replies posted under it in the meantime are lost with it.
LIMITATIONS: No child replies, sibling comments or parent-comment nesting existed, so 'siblings and parent untouched' and the cascade/'removed placeholder' behaviour for a comment that has children were NOT tested. Moderator deletion of another user's comment (different control/path than delete_own) not tested. Deletion is irreversible in-app: forum Trash and moderation log remained empty, so a deleted comment cannot be restored — the reverter is only valid for undoing a comment the agent itself created. Threaded-reply variant (Reply on a parent comment, textarea #reply_to_comment_<PARENT_ID>_comment) was not exercised; only the submission-level comment form was.

VERIFIED SCOPE ONLY: Verified only: create-one-forum then delete-that-forum on Postmill, pinned by exact forum name, as the forum's owner/moderator. Single fixture forum with no submissions, comments, subscribers other than the creator, tags, bans or wiki pages. UNTESTED: deletion of a forum that has dependants (submissions/comments/other subscribers), deletion by a non-owner moderator or admin, cascade behaviour, name re-use timing beyond an immediate 200 on /create_forum, whether any global moderation log records the deletion, and any recovery for forum edit/appearance changes. Not applicable to other applications (ownCloud, GitLab) - not touched in this pass.
Undo a self-created Postmill forum by permanently deleting it, pinned by its exact forum name. Creation-only mutation with a native inverse: no pre-state content capture is needed, but the deletion is irreversible, so it is safe only for a forum the same run created. Presence must be checked with GET /f/<name> plus the /submit forum selector, not the ranked/paginated /forums list.
LIMITATIONS: Deletion is irreversible by design ('no way of reviving the data on this forum once it's gone'); the forum did not land in any Trash, so this inverse is safe ONLY for a forum the same run created - never for pre-existing/shared forums. Presence cannot be checked from /forums page 1 (ranked/paginated listing did not show the brand-new forum even while it existed); use GET /f/<name> status plus the /submit selector. Playwright CSS locators scoped by form ('form:has(#forum_name) button[type=submit]', 'main form button[type=submit]') time out on Postmill's markup; text-based button locators via browser_click were required. Only one forum was exercised; no assertion is made that this inverse is exhaustive for forums with content or multiple moderators.

commands: navigate to /f/<name> for the forum whose name == '<name>' and confirm the acting account is its owner/moderator
delete that forum through its Edit forum / delete affordance, accepting confirmation
verify /forums and the /submit forum dropdown no longer list '<name>'; never delete any pre-existing or shared forum

patterns.skill:
VERIFIED SCOPE ONLY: (a) one text+URL submission owned by the acting user, edited and restored through the web edit form; (b) one comment body edited and restored, with one child reply as the only dependency checked. Untested: submission comments/child dependants (the 'comments unaffected' claim is NOT verified for submission edits), image submissions, forum reassignment, moderator editing another user's post or comment, repeated edits, deletion/trash semantics, and any API-level restore.
Postmill has no revision history, diff or revert for submissions or comments, so capture the pre-state yourself before the edit is saved or the original content is unrecoverable. Always read raw form values (.value / inputValue), never rendered HTML, so the markdown source survives; also keep the rendered HTML for comparison.
SUBMISSION branch: goto /f/<FORUM>/<SUBMISSION_ID>/-/edit (note: /f/<FORUM>/<SUBMISSION_ID>/edit does NOT 404 — it renders the submission page and a naive capture there silently reads nothing) and read #submission_title, #submission_body and #submission_url via browser_run_code_unsafe; the edit form has no forum select, so forum needs no capture. To restore, re-open the same /-/edit URL, fill the captured values verbatim, click 'Edit submission', then re-read the form and the rendered title/body and compare byte-for-byte. A title change rewrites the canonical slug, so saved slug URLs break until the title is restored (the numeric-id URL keeps working).
COMMENT branch: record the comment permalink, the raw markdown in its edit-form textarea (#comment_comment at <COMMENT_PERMALINK>/edit) and the rendered .comment__body HTML. Restore by reopening <COMMENT_PERMALINK>/edit, writing the captured raw markdown back into the same textarea (browser_fill_form), clicking 'Save', then re-reading both the textarea value and the rendered HTML and comparing to the capture; also confirm child replies are still nested.
Both branches: recovery is content-complete but metadata-incomplete — the restore is itself an edit, so the byline's '(edited N minutes later)' marker and edit timestamp appear on the first edit and survive the restore.
LIMITATIONS: No revision history/diff/revert for Postmill submissions or comments — recovery is only possible from a pre-state captured from the edit form BEFORE the original edit. The '(edited N minutes later)' marker and edit timestamp are permanent residue (partial recovery). The submission edit form URL is /f/<FORUM>/<SUBMISSION_ID>/-/edit; the plausible /f/<FORUM>/<SUBMISSION_ID>/edit path renders the submission page instead. Title changes rewrite the canonical slug. Forum reassignment could not be tested (no forum select on the edit form). Comment check compared raw source and rendered HTML only; no broader metadata audit.

VERIFIED SCOPE ONLY: One Postmill comment with exactly one direct child, same author, single forum/submission, delete performed by the comment's own author via 'delete_own'. Untested: moderator delete of another user's comment, deeper/multi-page subtrees, comments with votes/flags/edited markers, deletion of a whole submission, Postmill-side purge of the tombstone, and any other application (ownCloud, GitLab) — none touched in this run.
Postmill has no undelete, revision history, Trash entry or moderation-log entry for comments, so recovery is capture-and-replay, not restoration. Before the delete, read each comment's raw markdown from its /-/comment/<CID>/edit textarea (it becomes 403 after deletion) together with author, timestamp, permalink, parent, and every descendant's raw body depth-first. To restore, POST the captured body as a new comment at the captured parent (submission-level form for a top-level comment; per-comment form for a nested one, which only exists in the DOM after clicking that comment's 'Reply' link), then replay each captured child under the newly issued parent id. Verify by reading the new comments' edit textareas back and comparing byte-for-byte against the capture plus scanning rendered nesting depth. Expect new ids/permalinks and new creation timestamps, and expect the original tombstone plus its orphaned children to remain in the database and in the thread counter — the restore duplicates the subtree rather than replacing it.
LIMITATIONS: Postmill offers no undelete, revision history, Trash entry or moderation-log entry for comments, so recovery is re-creation, not restoration. Recovery is partial by construction: new comment ids and permalinks are issued and the original creation timestamps are permanently lost; only body text, author (when the restorer is the original author), and nesting shape are reproducible. The delete leaves a permanent '[deleted]' tombstone plus the original orphaned child in the database — hidden from the thread view but live at its permalink and still counted by the thread comment counter; the UI offers no way to purge it, so restore duplicates the subtree rather than replacing it. Child replies cannot be re-parented, so surviving children must be replayed as new comments under the restored parent. The per-comment reply form (and its CSRF token) exists in the DOM only after clicking that comment's 'Reply' link; there is no GET-able /reply page (returned 404). Only browser/HTTP access was available (no DB or shell), so persistence beyond the rendered pages was not inspected.

VERIFIED SCOPE ONLY: Verified for the text settings on /f/<FORUM>/edit of a forum owned/moderated by the acting account, on a forum with no submissions. UNTESTED: /f/<FORUM>/appearance controls (never opened or changed), forum[name] slug rename and its URL/dependant effects, non-empty forum[email] values, behaviour with existing submissions/comments under the forum, concurrent-editor conflicts, and restoring a forum edited by a different user.
Postmill has no revision history, revert, or moderation-log entry for forum edits, so pre-edit values are unrecoverable from the application. Before saving /f/<FORUM>/edit, read every non-hidden control of form[name=forum] (name, title, description, sidebar, sidebar_markdown_help checkbox, tags, email) and persist the values verbatim. Restore by refilling the identical captured values and clicking 'Save changes', then re-read the edit form and diff field-by-field against the capture, and confirm the public forum page shows the original title, sidebar and tags.
LIMITATIONS: No native inverse exists in Postmill for forum edits — no revision history, diff, or revert; the per-forum moderation log records nothing for an edit, so pre-edit values are unrecoverable from the application unless captured externally first. Only the /edit tab was exercised; the Appearance tab of the same forum was not captured or restored, so the pattern's claim for appearance fields is unverified. Forum names must be unique ('A forum by that name already exists.'); a disposable forum created for testing needs a fresh name. Single-example verification; no claim of exhaustive recovery across forum types or field combinations.

VERIFIED SCOPE ONLY: Verified only: single-field text edit + write-back restore of the acting account's Postmill biography, plus a read-only capture/diff of the full preferences form. The recovery claim is 'capture-then-write-back restores the biography exactly, including its rendered dependant'.
Postmill has no revision history or revert for user biography/preferences, so capture is mandatory before the edit. Biography lives on /user/<USER>/edit_biography, not /user/<USER>/preferences — snapshot the textarea value there (and, if settings are in scope, every checkbox .checked / text .value / select .value on the preferences route) with browser_run_code_unsafe. Restore by refilling the exact captured string with browser_fill_form and clicking Save, then verify by re-reading the form AND the rendered profile page (captured value present, new value absent). Select Save by accessible name — a generic form button[type=submit] selector matches nav buttons and times out.
LIMITATIONS: The preferences form itself (checkboxes/selects) was captured and diffed but never mutated — restore of a toggle/select change is inferred from the identical capture/refill mechanism, not demonstrated. Postmill exposes no revision history, diff or revert for user biography/preferences, so pre-edit state is unrecoverable from the application if not captured externally beforehand. Only one text field was mutated; multi-field simultaneous edits, markdown-formatted bios, empty-string restore, and max-length/validation rejection paths were not tested. Selector caveat (not a recovery limitation): the page contains additional type=submit buttons in the nav (Dark mode, Light mode, Log out), so a generic 'form button[type=submit]' click times out; the Save button must be selected by accessible name. Untested scope: /user/<USER>/account (email/password), block_list, hidden_forums, user trash; other applications on the same browser server were not touched.

VERIFIED SCOPE ONLY: One submission-level vote transition (up -> none -> up) on a single disposable submission, using browser_click for both the original op and the restore. Untested scope: comment votes (form[action='/cv/<COMMENT_ID>'] - same markup, not exercised), up->down and down->up transitions, voting by a different user, vote state on listing pages vs permalink, and any ranking/hot-score side effects of voting.
Before clicking any vote arrow, capture the widget's per-user state from form[action='/sv/<SUBMISSION_ID>'] (or '/cv/<COMMENT_ID>'): className, data-vote-choice-value ('1'|'-1'|'0'), data-vote-score-value, .vote__net-score, button.vote__up/.vote__down title+value, and .submission-meta__score. To restore, click button.vote__up if the captured choice was '1', button.vote__down if '-1', or click the currently-active arrow once if '0'; then reload and assert className, data-vote-choice-value and .vote__net-score equal the captured values. Postmill has no vote history or undo, so an uncaptured pre-click state is unrecoverable from the application.
LIMITATIONS: Postmill's submission rate limit ('You cannot post more. Wait a while before trying again.') can block creating a fresh test submission; the verification reused an existing disposable submission rather than shared content. The pre-existing vote was the author's automatic self-upvote; a vote cast by an explicitly different prior action (e.g. a downvote) was not exercised. The displayed net score is global while the vote is per-user, so a concurrent third-party vote between capture and restore would break the score equality check even when the user's own vote is correctly restored. Postmill provides no vote history, moderation-log entry, or undo affordance; if the pre-click state is not captured it is unrecoverable from the application. The select2-wrapped forum <select> on /submit is aria-hidden, so Playwright selectOption fails; the value must be set via DOM evaluate. A beforeunload dialog fires on submit navigation.

VERIFIED SCOPE ONLY: Single forum subscription toggle for one account on one newly created disposable forum. Dependant checked: the account's subscribed-forum sidebar listing (proxy for the subscription list) on / and /subscribed.
Before clicking a forum's subscribe/unsubscribe control, capture the button's current label ('Subscribe' vs 'Unsubscribe'), its subscriber count and the form action on /f/<FORUM>. The control is a stateful toggle with no set-to-value action, so capture is required and the tested inverse is the toggle itself. Restore by clicking `form[action="/f/<FORUM>/<subscribe|unsubscribe>"] button` only if the current label differs from the captured one; verify label + subscriber count on the forum page and the forum's membership in the account's 'Subscribed forums' sidebar on / and /subscribed.
LIMITATIONS: /subscriptions and /forums/subscribed return 404 in the tested Postmill build, so a '/subscriptions listing' check must be substituted with the 'Subscribed forums' sidebar on / and /subscribed. Front-page feed *post composition* was not diffed before/after — the test forum had no submissions, so feed content could not change; only listing membership was verified. Untested: subscribing to a forum not owned by the account (shared forums), multi-forum batch restore, subscription ordering/timestamp fields, and whether an unsubscribe/resubscribe cycle alters any hidden 'subscribed since' value not exposed in the UI. Verified only for the logged-in acting account's session; no other account's view checked. The disposable test forum was left in place (subscribed, matching capture); no cleanup deletion attempted.

VERIFIED SCOPE ONLY: One forum-scoped ban applied and reverted in a self-owned disposable forum. Untested scope: the trash/restore variant of the same pattern (blocked, see limitations), timed/expiring bans, global (site-wide) bans, moderator add/remove recovery, whether the unbanned user regains posting ability (not exercised as that user), multi-ban lists, and bans in forums not owned by this account.
Before banning, capture the forum's /f/<FORUM>/bans table, /f/<FORUM>/moderation_log and the sidebar Moderators list. Recover with the native inverse Unban at /f/<FORUM>/unban/<USERNAME> (a mandatory free-text reason is required), then diff the rendered Bans table and Moderators list against the capture — a clean revert returns the bans table byte-identical to the capture (e.g. 'There are no entries to display.' when it was empty). State explicitly that the moderation log and /f/<FORUM>/bans/history/<USERNAME> keep both the ban and the unban rows with no delete control: recovery restores enforcement state only, never the audit trail. Note that /f/<FORUM>/bans/new and /f/<FORUM>/bans/<USERNAME> are 404 — the ban entry point is /f/<FORUM>/ban/<USERNAME>.
LIMITATIONS: Trash/restore half of the pattern could NOT be tested: Postmill refused every submission with 'You cannot post more. Wait a while before trying again.' across repeated waits and also for a brand-new account from the same browser — an IP-level submission rate limit — so no submission existed to trash in the test forum. Moderation-log and ban-history entries are permanent residue: recovery restores enforcement state only, not the audit trail. Unban requires a mandatory free-text reason, so the restore itself writes a second permanent log entry. Dependant 'banned user's ability to post' was inferred from the bans table, not re-exercised by logging in as the banned user after the unban. Test residue stays behind: the disposable forum and the throwaway ban-target account (Postmill exposes no user deletion to a non-admin); the forum name field is capped in length, so disposable names must be short.

VERIFIED SCOPE ONLY: One small text file on one ownCloud account via WebDAV PUT with Basic auth. Content + checksum + size recovery only, on an unshared, untagged, unfavourited file.
Overwrite is not self-inverting: ownCloud keeps no recoverable handle to the previous bytes through the write itself, so capture before the write. GET the full bytes from /remote.php/dav/files/<USER>/<PATH> with Basic auth and stream them to an artifact file (never hold them only in context), and record PROPFIND Depth:0 metadata (getcontentlength, getetag, getlastmodified, oc:checksums, oc:fileid) plus the OCS share list for the path. Restore by PUTting the captured bytes back to the identical path, then re-GET and re-PROPFIND and compare raw body, size and SHA1/MD5 against the capture. Content, size and checksums recover exactly; ETag and mtime do not, and each PUT (mutation and restore) appends a version entry under /remote.php/dav/meta/<FILEID>/v that cannot be pruned — report both as residue. A native version-rollback inverse exists (COPY from the meta versions collection) but was not exercised here.
LIMITATIONS: ETag and last-modified are not restorable — any consumer keyed on ETag/mtime sees a changed resource. Version history grows monotonically; the overwrite and the restore each add a version entry and none can be pruned through the tested surface. Native version-rollback inverse (COPY /remote.php/dav/meta/<FILEID>/v/<VERSION_TS> onto the live path, or the versions UI) was observed to exist (207 listing with prior revisions) but was NOT executed. Shares, favourites and tags were not exercised: the test file had no share (OCS data []), no tag, no favourite, so preservation of those dependants across an overwrite is untested. Only a small text file was used; chunked/large-file upload and the browser_file_upload UI path (the pattern's applies_to) were not exercised — verification used the equivalent WebDAV PUT the upload performs. Playwright script sandbox lacks the Buffer global (Buffer.from threw); base64 decoding of the capture had to happen outside the sandbox, so a true binary restore needs the bytes re-encoded on the agent side or a file-backed PUT.

VERIFIED SCOPE ONLY: One folder with a few immediate child files, no shares, no tags/favourites, no version history, single level of nesting, same-user restore to the original path, restored shortly after deletion.
A folder delete in ownCloud moves the whole subtree to the trashbin as one entry, so the native inverse is a trashbin restore of that entry — no re-upload needed. Before deleting, capture a recursive PROPFIND (path, size, etag, fileid, oc:checksums) of the target, download each descendant's bytes, and query OCS shares?path=<PATH>&reshares=true&subfiles=true; this capture is needed only to diff after recovery, not to perform it. To recover, list the trashbin via /index.php/apps/files_trashbin/ajax/list.php, find the entry whose name is <TARGET_NAME>.d<DELETE_TIMESTAMP>, POST it to files_trashbin/ajax/undelete.php with dir=/ from the authenticated page context (the requesttoken is required; the Files-view Restore button posts the same call), then PROPFIND Depth: infinity and GET each child to confirm the subtree, sizes, fileids, etags and SHA1s match the capture. Restore to the original path preserves fileids and etags exactly; oc:checksums metadata was observed to be absent afterwards even though content was byte-identical. Note that /remote.php/dav/trash-bin/... does not exist on the tested ownCloud 10 build — use the files_trashbin ajax endpoints. Never touch unrelated pre-existing trash entries.
LIMITATIONS: The ownCloud Files web list did not render in the browser session ('Problem loading page, reloading in 5 seconds'; #fileList had 0 rows across reloads) even though /index.php/apps/files/ajax/list.php returned 200, so the Deleted-files 'Restore' button could not be clicked; the exact endpoint that button posts to (files_trashbin/ajax/undelete.php with requesttoken) was invoked from the same authenticated page context instead. Share restoration untested: the test folder had no shares, so the claim that share ids are dropped and must be re-issued is NOT verified here. Version history, tags and favourites on descendants were not created, so their survival through delete/restore is untested. Deeper nesting, paginated/large listings, name-collision on restore, trashbin retention expiry, and the re-upload fallback path (when the trash entry is absent) were not exercised. oc:checksums absence after restore was observed on the tested build only; not probed further. Unrelated pre-existing trashbin entries (other users' or earlier deletions) must be left untouched; only the entry for the target is restored.

VERIFIED SCOPE ONLY: One ownCloud file-type trashbin entry, a disposable file owned by the acting user, original location at the account root, single-entry 'Delete permanently' via the row Actions menu, restore by WebDAV PUT of the captured bytes with SHA1/size comparison.
Capture before purging: the trashbin DAV endpoint does not exist on the tested ownCloud 10 build, so enumerate entries with GET /index.php/apps/files_trashbin/ajax/list.php?dir=%2F (name, size, mtime = delete timestamp, extraData = original location), then obtain the bytes via a restore → download → re-delete round trip (UI 'Restore' click; the undelete.php ajax POST with a plain filename fails), storing the body plus PROPFIND fileid/size/oc:checksums and the recorded original path. Recover by PUTting the captured bytes to that original path over WebDAV and verifying getcontentlength and SHA1. Recovery is content-level only: fileid, trash entry id, delete timestamp and version history are unrecoverable. Never bulk-purge ('Empty deleted files') a trashbin that holds entries you do not own.
LIMITATIONS: The WebDAV trashbin endpoint (/remote.php/dav/trashbin/<USER>/trash) is unavailable on the tested ownCloud 10 build, so trash bytes cannot be downloaded directly; capture requires a restore-download-redelete round trip, which briefly makes the entry live and changes its delete timestamp. POST /index.php/apps/files_trashbin/ajax/undelete.php with the display filename failed ('Couldn't restore'); the internal '<name>.d<timestamp>' form was not determined in this run, so programmatic restore was not established here - only the UI Restore click. 'Empty deleted files' (bulk purge) was NOT executed: the trashbin held many entries owned by others and a bulk purge would destroy them; only single-entry purge is verified. Only a small text file was tested: no folder trash entry, no multi-version file, no shared file, no large/chunked upload, no non-root original path. Version history was not populated before deletion, so 'version history is unrecoverable after purge' is asserted from the restored file having no versions, not from losing an observed multi-version chain. fileid, trash entry id and deletion timestamp are unrecoverable through any browser-reachable interface; no occ CLI, database or server filesystem access was available to verify otherwise. Recovery is content-level only and demonstrated on one entry; exhaustive recovery of a whole trashbin (pagination, folders, conflicts on re-upload) is untested.

VERIFIED SCOPE ONLY: Verified on ownCloud only, on one disposable folder, for: user share (share_type 0) permission PUT + restore, and public link share (share_type 3) create/revoke/re-create with password. Single share page (a couple of rows) — pagination not exercised.
Shares have no trash or undo, so capture is mandatory before any share mutation. Capture with GET /ocs/v1.php/apps/files_sharing/api/v1/shares?format=json&path=<PATH>&reshares=true (headers: Authorization Basic, OCS-APIRequest: true) — do NOT add subfiles=true, which returns data [] for a folder's own shares. Record per share: id, share_type, share_with, permissions, expiration, token, url, and whether a password is set; link passwords are only readable as a bcrypt hash and must be re-supplied by the user. Restore a surviving share by PUTting the captured permissions back onto its id — this is exact. A revoked share can only be re-created (POST), which yields a NEW id, NEW token and NEW public URL; the old URL is permanently 404. Verify by re-running the capture GET and diffing field-by-field, and check old-link liveness with GET /index.php/s/<TOKEN> (303 alive / 404 dead).
LIMITATIONS: Expiry could not be captured or restored on the tested instance: PUT expireDate=<DATE> -> statuscode 400 'Wrong or no update parameter given' (capabilities files_sharing.public.expire_date.enabled=false). Expiry restore is UNTESTED. Link password plaintext is unrecoverable from the API (bcrypt hash only) — recovery is partial and requires the user to re-supply it. Revoked share recovery is re-creation, not restoration: new share id, new token, new public URL; any distributed old URL is permanently dead. No trash/undo exists for shares. Not tested: group shares (share_type 1), federated shares (6), share 'name' field, resharing chains, notifying/verifying the recipient's own 'Shared with you' view, multi-page share lists, and restoring a share onto a path that was itself deleted. The recipient was a pre-existing account; its account settings were not modified, only the share grant on the disposable folder.

VERIFIED SCOPE ONLY: One file, one same-owner move within the user's own tree, one dependant (public-link share). Shows MOVE is an exact lossless inverse and share bindings survive both directions.
Before the move, capture the source path plus fileid/ETag/size/permissions/favorite/tags via PROPFIND Depth:0, and the OCS share records whose path equals the source path. To restore, PROPFIND the source path first to confirm it is free (404), then WebDAV MOVE the item from its current path back to the captured source path with Overwrite: F, and verify with PROPFIND on both paths (source 207 with the captured fileid/ETag/size, destination 404), a GET for byte-identical content, and a refetch of the captured share. Capture is required for the source path string and for the comparison values, but share re-creation is not: on the tested ownCloud 10 build a share binds to fileid, so its path is rewritten by the move and rewritten back by the inverse MOVE, with id, token, permissions and file_source unchanged.
LIMITATIONS: Single small text file; folder/collection moves, cross-storage moves and moves in/out of a received share untested. Only share_type 3 tested; user (0), group (1), federated shares unverified. favorite/tags captured but were unset/empty — their survival untested. Original op ran via WebDAV API, not a UI drag/rename browser_click (same server-side MOVE). Collision case (source path re-occupied at restore) checked for but never provoked. Versioning/trashbin not involved in a move, so those paths remain unverified.

VERIFIED SCOPE ONLY: One ownCloud folder created by MKCOL at the account root and reverted. Untested scope: PUT-created files, nested/non-root paths, folders created with content or children, ownCloud 'New' menu / browser_click UI path (only the WebDAV verb was exercised), created objects that acquire shares/favourites/tags/versions before revert, other users' or group-shared targets, and Postmill/GitLab creation inverses.
Creation at a previously non-existent ownCloud path has a native inverse and needs no pre-state capture — but a plain WebDAV DELETE is not a full revert, because ownCloud moves the deleted object into the trashbin and leaves a lingering copy plus an extra trash entry. Full revert = DELETE the exact created path, then purge only that one resulting trash entry. Pin the path: confirm (PROPFIND 404 before creation, 207 after) that the target is the entity just created, so DELETE can never destroy pre-existing content. Scope the purge by diffing the trash listing before and after the DELETE and purging only the newly appeared entry, whose id is the composed name `<basename>.d<unix_ts>` with the timestamp read from that entry's mtime (milliseconds, converted to seconds). On this build the WebDAV trashbin endpoints are absent (404), so enumeration and purge go through the legacy files_trashbin ajax endpoints, and the purge POST requires a CSRF requesttoken read from a logged-in browser page (window.oc_requesttoken) — HTTP Basic auth alone is rejected for it, so the reverter is not purely header-auth scriptable. Verify by re-checking PROPFIND on the path (404), the parent listing href count back to its initial value, and that every pre-existing trash (name|mtime) pair is still present.
LIMITATIONS: WebDAV trashbin access is unavailable on the tested build: PROPFIND /remote.php/dav/trashbin/<USER>/ and /remote.php/dav/trash-bin/<USER>/trash/ both return 404; trash enumeration and purge required the legacy files_trashbin ajax endpoints. Purging the trash entry needs a CSRF requesttoken read from a logged-in browser page (window.oc_requesttoken); HTTP Basic auth alone is rejected for that POST, so the reverter is not purely header-auth scriptable. Trash purge targets the composed name '<basename>.d<unix_ts>'; the timestamp must be read from the trash listing (its mtime is in milliseconds; divide to seconds). Loading /index.php/apps/files/?dir=/&view=trashbin with waitUntil:'load' timed out at 30s (domcontentloaded works). Sibling non-interference verified at parent-listing granularity (href count + absence of target) and by full trash name|mtime comparison, not per-sibling etag/content. Only the folder (MKCOL) variant was executed; PUT/file and UI 'New' variants are inferred, not verified.

VERIFIED SCOPE ONLY: One file, one favourite flag plus a one-element tag set, on one ownCloud account, via WebDAV properties. Untested scope: the star click in the Files web UI (browser_click) and the Tags web view; multi-tag sets and tag ordering; system tags with non-default scope (static/assignable) and the /systemtags OCS API; tags on folders; other users' or shared files; whether deleting the tag itself (vs unassigning) is recoverable; concurrent tag edits; any other file metadata (shares, versions, trashbin) — untouched.
There is no native undo or version history for tag/favourite metadata, so capture is mandatory: before the change, PROPFIND Depth 0 on the file for oc:favorite and oc:tags (plus oc:fileid/getetag for identity). Recover by PROPPATCH-setting exactly the captured favourite value and the captured tag list back, then re-run the capture PROPFIND and diff, and re-run the Favorites REPORT on the parent collection to confirm the dependent view. Send favourite and tags in the same PROPPATCH only when the captured tag set is non-empty (tested form); clearing tags requires a single empty <oc:tag></oc:tag> rather than d:remove.
LIMITATIONS: The ownCloud Files web UI file list did not render in the browser session (banner 'Problem loading page, reloading in 5 seconds'; #fileList had 0 rows across repeated reload attempts, one navigation aborted by the auto-reload), so the pattern's browser_click star path was NOT exercised — capture, mutation and recovery were all performed over WebDAV PROPFIND/PROPPATCH. A combined PROPPATCH setting oc:favorite=0 and an empty <oc:tags/> in one request returns HTTP 500 and applies nothing (favourite remained set) — favourite and tags must be sent in separate requests. <d:remove><d:prop><oc:tags/></d:prop></d:remove> returns HTTP 500 (HTML error page) and is a no-op; clearing tags requires setting oc:tags to a single empty <oc:tag></oc:tag>. No native undo/history exists for tag or favourite assignment (no versioning of metadata), so recovery depends entirely on a pre-mutation capture; if the original operation runs without capture, the prior tag set is unrecoverable from the application. Tag removal here was unassignment only; whether the system tag object itself survived deletion was not tested (the tag still resolved on re-assign, which is consistent but not proof).

VERIFIED SCOPE ONLY: One minimal disposable project in the acting admin's personal namespace, no dependants (no issues/MRs/branches beyond the initial README commit, no members, no wiki content). Verified only the API delete inverse on GitLab CE personal-namespace projects; single application, single object, single run.
Creating a GitLab project is creation-only: no pre-state content needs capturing, only the new project's identity (id, path_with_namespace, created_at) at creation time. The tested inverse is an authenticated REST DELETE of that project, guarded by re-reading the project and asserting its path_with_namespace and created_at match the captured values, so a same-named pre-existing project can never be hit. API writes succeed with the browser session cookie plus the X-CSRF-Token from meta[name=csrf-token]; no personal access token is required. Note for the forward op: the /projects/new blank-project form silently no-ops on submit until a namespace is chosen, with no validation message — the namespace picker must be set before clicking 'Create project'.
LIMITATIONS: The /projects/new blank-project form silently no-ops on submit until a namespace is chosen — no validation message; submit clicks were consumed before this was diagnosed. Any reuse of the create recipe must include the namespace-picker step. Group-namespace projects untested: group settings can enable delayed deletion, where DELETE only sets marked_for_deletion_at instead of hard-deleting. Cascade behaviour untested: the project had no issues, MRs, extra branches, members, forks, wiki pages, packages or CI data at delete time. The UI inverse (Settings > Advanced > Delete project type-to-confirm form) was not exercised; only the REST API inverse was. Path reuse / re-creation after delete not attempted; deletion of forks or LFS-bearing projects not attempted. Correction to prior environment note: API writes DO succeed with session cookie + X-CSRF-Token header; no PAT is needed (none was created).

VERIFIED SCOPE ONLY: One minimal disposable issue (title only: no description, labels, assignee, milestone, notes, attachments) created via the genuine New-issue UI submit in an existing project and deleted immediately. Pin is iid (project-scoped); project_id + iid is the substitutable identity. No dependants existed at creation, and none were added, per creation-only guidance.
Creating a GitLab issue through the New-issue UI is creation-only and has a native inverse: no pre-state artifact is needed, only the created object's identity (project_id + iid; global id incidental). Recover by permanently deleting that issue via DELETE /api/v4/projects/<project_id>/issues/<iid>, authenticated by the existing GitLab session cookie PLUS the page's meta[name=csrf-token] value sent as X-CSRF-Token — session cookie alone is rejected for REST write verbs, so a same-origin GitLab page must be loaded in the tab first. This is the API form of the issue page's Delete action, not close/hide/archive. Pin the iid (project-scoped), guard the delete by re-reading the issue and confirming the title this run typed, and confirm recovery with a 404 on the API and web page plus the opened-issue X-Total returning to its pre-action value. Verified on the tested GitLab CE 17 build as the instance admin (Owner/Admin required) on a title-only issue with no dependants.
LIMITATIONS: GitLab REST write verbs are rejected on the session cookie alone; the DELETE only worked with the page CSRF token (no PAT was created), so the reverter requires a same-origin GitLab page to be loaded first. Deletion requires Owner/Admin rights; verified only as the instance admin. Untested: issues carrying notes/comments, award emoji, linked MRs, attachments, designs or board placement (cascade behaviour on delete unverified); issues created via API instead of UI; non-admin actors; other projects/groups; iid reuse after deletion; whether the deletion is logged or recoverable anywhere (no tombstone/undo checked); bulk creation. Count check relies on the X-Total header of the opened-issues endpoint, not a UI badge.

VERIFIED SCOPE ONLY: Verified only on a purpose-built disposable issue in a disposable project, as an administrator. Verified fields: title, description, labels, assignee_ids, milestone_id, state (close→reopen). Untested scope: UI-form-based restore (restore was done via API PUT, not the edit form), close/reopen performed through the UI dropdown, non-empty assignee/milestone restore, due date, weight, confidentiality, issue type, linked/related items, board position, labels that must pre-exist in another project, non-admin permissions, and resource_state_events (close/reopen events are not in /notes and were not fetched). No shared project or account state was touched.
GitLab issue field edits have no native undo or revision history, so capture before saving: GET /api/v4/projects/<PROJECT_ID>/issues/<IID> and record title, raw description, labels[], assignees[].id, milestone.id and state. Restore by PUTting those exact values back to the same endpoint (labels as a comma-joined string, assignee_ids array, milestone_id, state_event reopen/close to undo a state flip). API writes need the page CSRF token (meta[name="csrf-token"]) in addition to the session cookie — cookie-only writes fail; GET works with the cookie alone. Verify by re-GETting and diffing every captured field. Recovery of values is complete, but the audit trail is not: each edit and the restore itself append permanent system notes to the issue, and updated_at advances on every write.
LIMITATIONS: Partial recovery: field values are fully restorable, but the audit trail is not — each edit and the restore itself append permanent system notes to the issue; there is no API/UI to delete system notes. updated_at cannot be restored (advances on every write). GitLab API writes require the page CSRF token (or a PAT) in addition to the session cookie; cookie-only writes fail. The UI 'Close issue' control lives in the work-item actions dropdown and was not clickable with selectors button:has-text("Close issue") / [data-testid="state-toggle-action"]; close was therefore issued via API PUT state_event, so the browser_click trigger for close/reopen remains unverified. Close/reopen produced no entries in /notes (GitLab records them as resource_state_events); that endpoint was not queried, so state-change trail permanence is unconfirmed.

VERIFIED SCOPE ONLY: One issue note in one disposable project on the tested GitLab CE build, with one threaded reply as the only dependant. Both branches of the pattern exercised once: UI delete + re-post restore, and API edit + PUT-back restore. Untested scope: merge-request notes, diff/position-anchored notes, system notes, notes by other authors, resolvable-thread resolved state, awards/emoji reactions on a note, attachments/uploads inside a note body, internal (confidential) notes, notifications/todos generated by the re-post, deleting an entire discussion or an issue, pagination beyond one page of notes, and non-admin permission behaviour.
GitLab notes have no history, trash or revert, so capture before acting: GET /api/v4/projects/<PID>/issues/<IID>/discussions?per_page=<MAX_PAGE_SIZE> (page through) to record each note's id, discussion_id, author, created_at/updated_at and raw body — /issues/<IID>/notes omits discussion_id on the tested build and is not sufficient. If the note still exists, restore it natively with PUT .../notes/<NOTE_ID> {body:<captured>}, which preserves id and created_at but bumps updated_at and leaves a permanent 'Edited … by X' marker. If the note was deleted, re-post the captured body with POST .../discussions/<DISCUSSION_ID>/notes, which yields a NEW note id and created_at appended to the end of the discussion (ordering versus surviving replies is not restored, and author attribution only holds if the same account re-posts). Verify by re-GETting /discussions and strict-comparing bodies and ordering against the capture, reporting any new note id/timestamp. Writes need the page CSRF token with the session cookie.
LIMITATIONS: Note deletion in GitLab is permanent: no trash, tombstone, undo or version history for notes, so the pre-delete body is unrecoverable from the application — the external capture is mandatory. Delete recovery is re-creation, not true restore: the restored note gets a NEW id and a NEW created_at, and it is appended to the discussion, so its position relative to a surviving reply is inverted versus the capture. Original author attribution was preserved only because the same account re-posted. Edit recovery is content-complete but metadata-partial: body matches byte-for-byte and id/created_at are kept, but updated_at is bumped and the UI shows a permanent 'Edited … by <USER>' marker with no diff/revert UI to clear it. On the tested build GET /issues/<IID>/notes returned notes without a discussion_id field, so a capture taken only from /notes would be insufficient to re-post into the original discussion; /discussions must be used. Writes require the page CSRF token with the session cookie (no PAT was minted); recovery therefore depends on an authenticated browser context. Edited-marker and re-post behaviour verified on a single note each; no claim of exhaustive recovery.

VERIFIED SCOPE ONLY: One branch in one freshly created disposable project, one dependent open MR, one branch-only commit, protection applied at Maintainer level. Recovery claim covers: branch ref at an exact SHA, its branch-only commit/content, protection level, and reopening an MR closed by the deletion — all via the GitLab REST API v4 driven in-page with the existing session cookie + X-CSRF-Token.
GitLab has no native undelete for branches, so capture before deleting: the branch name, its exact HEAD commit SHA, merged/protected flags, the protected-branch rule levels, and the list of open MRs sourced from the branch. Restore by re-creating the same branch name at the captured SHA; the protected-branch rule survives the deletion (re-protect returns 409 'already exists'), but MRs closed by the deletion are closed asynchronously and must be reopened explicitly with state_event=reopen. Verify by comparing the restored branch commit.id and branch-only file content_sha256 against the capture. Restore is only possible while the orphaned commit object still exists — it is fetchable by SHA after deletion but unreachable, so 'Prune unreachable objects' housekeeping can make the loss permanent.
LIMITATIONS: Restore depends entirely on the commit SHA being captured BEFORE deletion and on the object not yet being pruned; 'Prune unreachable objects' housekeeping was identified but deliberately NOT run, so the retention window and the post-prune failure mode are unverified. MR closure is asynchronous, so a capture/verify taken immediately after deletion can misreport MR state as still 'opened'. Re-creating the branch does not auto-reopen MRs; reopen was a separate explicit call. Only the open/closed state and source_branch were compared — MR discussion notes, approvals, diff versions and the merge-request-diff after branch loss were not compared. Deletion of a protected branch was allowed here because the actor is an administrator; the 403-then-unprotect path for Developer/Maintainer-restricted roles was not exercised. Tested only on a branch with no CI pipelines, no tags, no deploy keys/environments and no forks; cascade to those objects is untested. Only the API transport was exercised. The pattern's applies_to browser_click (UI 'Delete branch' button on /-/branches) was not clicked; the UI is expected to hit the same endpoint but that equivalence is unverified.

VERIFIED SCOPE ONLY: One minimal project holding one branch/commit, one issue with one note, and one wiki page. Untested scope (present in the export manifest but not exercised): merge requests with diffs, labels, milestones, snippets, LFS objects, issue boards, design management, CI/CD variables, integrations (explicitly excluded from GitLab export), deploy keys, project members/permissions, uploads, multi-page pagination of branches/issues/wikis, and non-personal (group) namespaces. Archive and change-path variants of the pattern were not tested — only permanent delete + export/import restore.
GitLab CE 17 deletes a project permanently and immediately (202, then 404 within seconds) — there is no trash, no marked_for_deletion_at and no undelete, so recovery is impossible unless a project export tarball was captured BEFORE the delete. Before the action: capture project settings, branches, issues (per_page=<MAX_PAGE_SIZE>) and wiki pages with content via the API, then POST /export, poll until export_status=='finished' and GET /export/download (retry once on 429). Restore by POST /api/v4/projects/import with the tarball, polling /import until finished, then re-run the same four GETs and diff. Report the unavoidable changes: the project gets a NEW id and issues get new backend ids (iids, titles, branch SHAs, settings and the URL path are preserved — the path only because the original was fully deleted). All writes need X-CSRF-Token from meta[name=csrf-token]; the session cookie alone is GET-only. Never run this against pre-existing shared projects.
LIMITATIONS: No native undelete/trash in GitLab CE 17: recovery is impossible without the export tarball captured BEFORE the delete; the delete itself is immediate (202, 404 within seconds). GET /api/v4/projects/<id>/export/download is rate limited — the first attempt returned 429 (a short JSON error); a retry returned 200. Restore creates a NEW project id and new backend issue ids; only iids, titles, SHAs and settings are preserved. The URL path was reusable only because the original project was fully deleted. API writes need the page CSRF token (session cookie is GET-only); no PAT was created. crypto.subtle is unavailable on a plain-http origin, so the tarball SHA-256 was computed off-browser after transfer; require/Buffer are unavailable in the Playwright code sandbox, so the tarball could not be written directly to the agent's filesystem — it was carried as base64 through localStorage (restore path) and through the tool result (archival copy). The archival copy carried over text had a few corrupted base64 characters (gzip CRC error); it was located by chunk checksum against the browser copy and repaired, then verified. The verified restore used the in-browser copy.

patterns.action: change settings / submit a form-backed record (Save)
patterns.skill:
VERIFIED SCOPE ONLY: Branch A: one disposable project's visibility setting on the tested GitLab CE build via the Settings>General form, restored via form and via authenticated API PUT; members and protected-branch lists observed as unchanged dependants (single owner, single rule, single page). Branch B: one application (Postmill), one form type (submission edit), text/url/select controls only, one disposable record. Untested scope: checkbox/radio/file controls (excluded from capture — the file input and hidden CSRF token cannot be captured/replayed), multi-page or wizard forms, form replay on ownCloud and GitLab, concurrent edits, comment/forum/user-preferences forms, and any dependants (no child comments were created, so cascade/keyed-off-field dependants were not exercised).
Neither application keeps undo/history for a saved form, so capture BEFORE the save is mandatory. Choose the restore path by what the app exposes:
(A) The app has an API for the same settings (verified on GitLab project settings): GET /api/v4/projects/<id> (visibility, all *_access_level, default_branch, merge settings), /members/all and /protected_branches (all pages) before saving. Restore authoritatively with an authenticated PUT /api/v4/projects/<id> writing EVERY captured field back (X-CSRF-Token from meta[name=csrf-token]) — do NOT rely on the Settings>General form inverse, which resubmits every feature select with its currently-rendered (visibility-clamped) value and silently downgrades enabled -> private. Members: PUT /members/<USER_ID> {access_level,expires_at}; removed members need POST /members re-invite (new membership record); protected branches via DELETE+POST (these member/rule branches are untested). Then re-GET project, members and protected_branches and diff field-by-field against the capture; updated_at always differs and is not restorable.
(B) The form is the only write path (verified on a Postmill edit form): before filling, read every non-hidden, non-file control's current value on the target form (inputs, textareas, selects) via browser_run_code_unsafe and store them keyed by control name; restore by re-opening the identical form URL (resolve it by immutable id, not by a slug derived from a mutated field), refilling exactly the captured values with browser_fill_form, submitting (click the submit button by its literal label; generic submit selectors timed out), then re-reading the form and diffing control-by-control against the capture. Field content restores byte-exactly; edit-provenance (e.g. an '(edited N later)' marker) does not.
LIMITATIONS: Branch A: updated_at cannot be restored — every save leaves a timestamp marker. Branch A: form-based restore is lossy: saving the visibility section rewrites all feature access levels with the currently-rendered (clamped) values, so a form-only inverse silently downgrades enabled -> private; full fidelity required the API PUT with the captured values. Branch A: member access_level/expires_at restore and member re-invite were NOT executed (the project had only its owner); the claim that a removed member returns as a new membership record is from the pattern, untested. Branch A: protected-branch rule rewrite (DELETE+POST) was NOT executed — rules were only captured and diffed as unchanged. Branch A: only visibility was mutated; default_branch, merge settings, deploy keys, tokens, and other General-settings sections were captured/diffed but not independently mutated and restored. Branch A: single-page lists only (one member, one protected branch); multi-page pagination of the capture is untested. Branch A: deploy keys / project-scoped tokens as dependants of a visibility change were not inventoried or tested. Branch B: partial recovery only: field content restores byte-exactly, but the '(edited N minutes later)' marker and the edit timestamp persist — Postmill has no revision history, diff or revert UI for submissions, so provenance cannot be returned to pre-edit state. Branch B: hidden inputs (submission[_token] CSRF) and file inputs (submission[image]) are deliberately excluded from the capture and are not restorable by this replay; an image-bearing submission's media could not be restored this way. Branch B: restore depends on the pre-mutation capture existing; if the original op runs before the capture, no application-side recovery path exists. Branch B: form-URL stability assumption: the edit URL is keyed by the record's numeric id, not the title slug, so the URL survived the title change — a form URL keyed by a mutated field would need re-resolution before restore.

VERIFIED SCOPE ONLY: Verified only: personal (non-project) GitLab snippet, single text file, small ASCII content, private visibility, owned by the administrator session, via REST API v4 with session cookie + CSRF token. Both branches of the pattern (edit-restore in place, delete-then-recreate) were exercised once each on one disposable snippet. Untested scope: project-scoped snippets (/api/v4/projects/<id>/snippets), multi-file snippets, file rename/move and delete actions within a snippet, binary/large content and encoding edge cases, non-owner or lower-privileged actors, public/internal visibility transitions, snippet comments/award emoji/discussion dependants, snippet git repo history or commit-level recovery, and web-UI (browser_click/browser_fill_form) edit/delete paths — all recovery here was driven through the API layer from an authenticated browser page.
Before editing or deleting a GitLab snippet, capture GET /api/v4/snippets/<id> (id, title, description, visibility, file_name, web_url, author, project_id, timestamps) and GET /api/v4/snippets/<id>/raw (verbatim bytes) to an external artifact — there is no trash, undelete or version-restore UI for snippets. To recover an edit, PUT the captured title/description/visibility plus files[{action:'update', file_path, previous_path, content:<captured raw>}] to the same id and byte-compare /raw against the capture. To recover a delete, POST a new snippet from the same capture: content is restored byte-for-byte but the id and all URLs change, so report the new id/URL. All write verbs from a logged-in browser page require the X-CSRF-Token from meta[name=csrf-token]; GETs do not.
LIMITATIONS: GitLab exposes no native inverse for snippets: no trash, no undelete, no revert/version-restore UI; deletion is immediate and permanent, so an external pre-capture is mandatory. updated_at cannot be restored — it always advances on the restoring PUT (partial recovery on timestamp metadata). Delete recovery is re-creation, not restoration: the original id is gone and unreusable; the restored object has a new id and new web/raw/git URLs, so any external references to the old id/URL break. API writes require the page CSRF token (session cookie alone yields 404 on write verbs); a restore run outside a logged-in browser page needs a personal access token instead. Snippet git history was not inspected, so it is unverified whether the pre-edit blob is independently recoverable from the snippet repository without the external capture. Single-sample demonstration — no claim of exhaustive recovery across snippet variants.

VERIFIED SCOPE ONLY: One personal access token on one GitLab instance, created and revoked through the UI (browser_click), verified by the read-only REST list endpoint. Dependants (automation authenticating with the token) were not exercised — the token was never used for any API call, so no consumer breakage was demonstrated.
Before acting, capture the token list from GET /api/v4/personal_access_tokens?per_page=100 with the session cookie (id, name, scopes, expires_at, created_at, revoked, active) and record that secret values are never readable. For a creation, record the new token's id from the post-create refetch and undo it with GitLab's native Revoke on exactly that id, then diff the refetched list against the capture to prove no other record changed. For a revocation, recovery is inherently partial: a replacement carries the captured name/scopes/expiry but a new id and a new secret, so every consumer must be re-configured — that direction was not executed.
LIMITATIONS: Only the creation direction was tested. The reverse direction (revoke an existing token, then mint a replacement with captured name/scopes/expiry) was NOT executed — that recovery is inherently partial because the secret value is unrecoverable and a replacement gets a new id plus a new secret, requiring every consumer to be re-configured. Untested claim, documented only. The one-time secret was shown but deliberately not persisted; token secrets can never be captured from the list API or UI. Revocation leaves a permanent revoked record (id remains, no purge affordance), so the 'active token set' returns to pre-state but the full record set does not. Deploy keys — the other object type named in the pattern — were not touched; only personal access tokens were verified. Verification used the session-cookie REST GET and the rendered table; no independent check that the revoked token is rejected at authentication time (no request was made with the token).

VERIFIED SCOPE ONLY: One live example: one ownCloud WebDAV text file, one verb (PUT overwrite) via page.request.fetch inside browser_run_code_unsafe, dependant-free resource. Untested: POST/PATCH/DELETE inverses (re-POST deleted record, DELETE created id), DOM form-submission variant, GitLab/Postmill scripted writes (GitLab writes need CSRF/PAT), binary/chunked payloads, multi-page PROPFIND paging, shares/tags/versions as dependants, ownCloud version history as alternative native inverse.
Before running a browser_run_code_unsafe snippet, parse it for the target URL and HTTP verb. For any non-GET/HEAD/PROPFIND/OPTIONS verb against a WebDAV resource, first PROPFIND Depth:0 (metadata) and GET (exact bytes) that same URL and persist both to an artifact file outside the browser. After the original write, restore by PUT-ing the captured bytes back to the same URL, then re-GET and re-PROPFIND to diff. Expect content to come back byte-identical and expect etag/getlastmodified to be newly minted — report those as not preserved. Compute Basic-auth base64 outside the script: the Playwright sandbox has no btoa/Buffer.
LIMITATIONS: Content recovery exact, metadata recovery partial: restore PUT mints a new etag and lastmodified; originals cannot be preserved via WebDAV PUT. No native inverse for overwrite-PUT; recovery depends entirely on the pre-capture — a scripted write executed without a prior GET is unrecoverable via this path. Only PUT-on-file exercised; id-pinned inverses for POST/DELETE not demonstrated. Playwright script sandbox lacks btoa/Buffer, so Basic-auth base64 was computed outside the browser.

VERIFIED SCOPE ONLY: One field, one record, one app for the positive claim: renaming an ownCloud folder's name via the inline rename input, plus the create-variant on the New-Folder input of the same app. Untested scope: ownCloud file (non-folder) renames, files with existing shares/versions/tags attached to the renamed node, name collisions and invalid-name rejection, concurrent editors, GitLab entirely, and Postmill restore-after-successful-edit (the op never mutated Postmill, so its restore leg was not exercised). Dependencies were deliberately not attached to the test folder; no dependant/child objects were involved in the recovery claim.
When submit=true will persist an edit, open the field first and capture both the live input value (page.$$eval on the field selector) and server truth (PROPFIND on the WebDAV node) before typing; there is no native undo. Restore by re-opening the same field on the mutated record (the row selector now keys on the mutated name) and retyping the captured value with submit=true, then re-read server truth to confirm the persisted value equals the capture. If the typed text created a brand-new record instead, no capture is needed — the tested inverse is a WebDAV DELETE of the created node. Do not assume the trigger mutates everywhere: on Postmill, Enter in a textarea only inserted a newline and Enter in #forum_title on /create_forum submitted nothing.
LIMITATIONS: browser_type submit=true is app- and element-dependent: on Postmill it mutated nothing — Enter in the title TEXTAREA (#submission_title) only inserted a newline, and Enter in the text INPUT #forum_title on /create_forum triggered no implicit submission. On Postmill the form must be submitted by clicking its submit button, so the 'type and submit' trigger cannot be assumed mutating there. Restore was verified on the field's persisted value only (name/path). Rename in ownCloud is a MOVE, so id/etag continuity was observed but share-, tag- and version-linkage after rename/restore was not re-verified. Postmill offers no revision history/diff/revert for submissions, so an actually-submitted Postmill edit remains unrecoverable without a prior external capture (capture step remains mandatory there) — this leg was not demonstrated end-to-end because the op did not submit. The ownCloud trashbin DAV endpoint /remote.php/dav/trashbin/<USER>/trash returned 404, so trash-level purge/restore of the test folder could not be exercised via WebDAV; cleanup relied on a plain WebDAV DELETE.

VERIFIED SCOPE ONLY: One live example only: Postmill image-submission upload of a single small new PNG into one test forum, recovered by the native submission Delete. Untested scope: the overwrite branch of the pattern (same-named file existing -> capture bytes and write them back) was NOT exercised anywhere; ownCloud UI upload and its versions/trash-restore semantics were not verified (UI upload was broken on the tested instance, see limitations); GitLab issue/MR attachment upload was not attempted at all; multi-file uploads, large/chunked uploads, share-state or version-history dependants, and upload into shared destinations were not tested.
Creation-only upload: before uploading, GET the destination listing and record the entry names. After the upload, record the created object URL and the server-side blob URL. Recover by deleting exactly the created object through the app's native Delete (accepting its confirm dialog) — in Postmill the blob's lifetime is coupled to the submission, so the blob 404s too. Then re-GET the object, the blob, the listing, the trash view and the moderation log and diff the listing against the capture. If a same-named file already exists at the destination, this is an overwrite, not a creation — that branch requires capturing the prior bytes first and was not exercised.
LIMITATIONS: ownCloud browser upload was non-functional on the tested build: #file_upload_start is hidden, the '+ New' toolbar container stays 'actions creatable hidden', and the Files app JS loops PROPFIND /remote.php/webdav/<dir> -> 401 Unauthorized, causing periodic self-reload. After force-unhiding the input, browser_click DID open the chooser and browser_file_upload setFiles succeeded, but no PUT was sent — the folder PROPFIND stayed empty and GET of the file returned 404. So browser_file_upload could not be verified on ownCloud; the ownCloud arm of the pattern is unavailable via the UI (WebDAV PUT remains a programmatic alternative, untested). ownCloud 10 has no trashbin DAV endpoint (PROPFIND /remote.php/dav/trashbin/<USER>/trash -> 404); purging a tombstone requires POST /index.php/apps/files_trashbin/ajax/delete.php with the page 'requesttoken' header and the trash name including its '.d<timestamp>' suffix. That endpoint returns status:success even for names that are not real trash entries, so a purge response is not evidence of deletion — re-list the Deleted files view to confirm (verified: live files named in a bad-name purge attempt were confirmed still present). Postmill rejects some valid PNGs ('The image file is corrupted.' for a tiny 1-bit grayscale PNG); a small 8-bit RGB PNG was accepted. Payload format constrains this upload op. Postmill's file input and the media-type radio are CSS-hidden, so browser_click on them times out; the chooser must be opened by clicking the radio's <label> first and then clicking the (now visible) file input with noWaitAfter — an extra browser_run_code_unsafe step before browser_file_upload. Recovery here relies on Postmill coupling blob lifetime to the submission (deleting the submission 404s the blob); this content-addressed blob is not separately addressable/deletable via the UI, so an app that keeps orphan blobs after object deletion would need a different inverse. Not generalizable beyond this app from one example. The uploaded blob's identity was matched by byte length and PNG header only — the Playwright sandbox has no Buffer/btoa/crypto and no require, so no server-side checksum was computed; the ownCloud OCS-advertised SHA1 checksum path was not used.

skill:
Backup guidance for browser services. Match application AND operation; use current instance URLs and stable IDs. Before mutation, save actual fields/bytes and affected dependents, with pagination. For an object with version history (state versions, file versions, page revisions), save every version with its order key, not only the latest. DOM snapshots or re-navigation do not undo server writes. Creation inverses target only new objects without later dependents. Capture now; do not execute the main destructive action. Verify restored content/state; IDs, timestamps and audit history may differ. Unmatched actions use generic backup guidance.

[1] Postmill create submission: pin new ID/permalink/title. For an own text post without dependents, Delete + confirm reverses creation; verify absence and prior listing. Other authors/types or existing comments are outside this scope.
[2] Postmill create comment: pin ID, parent and author. Delete_own + confirm reverses a new own top-level comment without replies; verify parent unchanged. Child-cascade recovery is unproven.
[3] Postmill create forum: pin new name and prior absence. Reverse at /f/<name>/delete with name confirmation only while empty. Existing posts/subscribers/dependents are excluded.
[4] Postmill edit own text (submission title/body/url or comment markdown): save the raw values from the record's edit form plus identity, parent/child relations and dependents; restore through the same edit form and compare values. Content/slug can return; edit timestamp/byline residue remains; rendered HTML alone is insufficient.
[5] Postmill delete comment: capture raw parent/child bodies, authors and nesting before delete. No native Trash restore was found; recreate captured comments in dependency order. Content/nesting can return with new IDs/times and tombstone/count residue; not identity-preserving recovery.
[6] Postmill edit forum: capture and restore /edit text settings. Tested title/description/sidebar/tags on an empty forum; appearance, slug rename and dependent content are excluded.
[7] Postmill biography: capture raw text, restore through edit_biography and compare profile/form. Preferences toggles were never mutated; this does not verify general account-setting recovery.
[8] Postmill vote: pin target and prior vote; restore through matching vote/retract controls. Tested submission up -> none -> up only, not comment or opposite-vote transitions.
[9] Postmill subscribe: pin forum and prior subscription; restore the toggle and compare subscribed listings. One account/forum only; notification settings are excluded.
[10] Postmill moderation: capture forum-scoped ban state and exact target, then restore that prior ban state with native controls. Only a disposable forum ban/unban was tested; trash restore, global bans, timed bans and moderator recovery are not established.
[11] ownCloud overwrite: GET the old file bytes and PROPFIND its identity/metadata before PUT. Persist and hash the bytes; restore by PUT and compare content/size. ETag, mtime, versions, shares and tags are not recovered merely by restoring content.
[12] ownCloud delete file/folder: recursively capture all descendant bytes, relative paths and metadata before DELETE. Prefer the trashbin restore of that entry; else recreate hierarchy with MKCOL/PUT and compare each file. Recreated identities and untested shares/tags/history remain limitations.
[13] ownCloud purge trash: download actual bytes and record original paths/metadata before permanent removal. Restore with MKCOL/PUT as needed and compare checksums. Recreated files do not preserve trash identity, timestamps or version history; a bin listing is insufficient.
[14] ownCloud share change: capture the complete share record and permissions before PUT, then restore captured values. For new public links, pin and revoke only that new share. Re-created secrets/tokens differ; expiry and undisclosed passwords are not proven recoverable.
[15] ownCloud MOVE/rename: pin source path, destination absence, file ID and dependent share bindings. Invert with MOVE to the saved source path and verify identity/content/share. Tested scope is a same-owner file move with one link share, not overwriting a destination.
[16] ownCloud create folder: pin new path and prior absence. DELETE reverses MKCOL only without subsequent content/dependents; verify absence. Existing folders and file overwrites are excluded.
[17] ownCloud favourite/tag: capture exact prior favourite flag and tag set plus file ID with WebDAV properties. Restore those properties and compare. Tested one-tag scope does not establish ordering, system-tag or every UI variant behavior.
[18] GitLab create project: pin new numeric ID and prior absence; delete that exact project only before later work/dependents accrue. Pre-existing or populated projects are excluded.
[19] GitLab create issue: pin project ID and new iid; delete that issue and verify absence. Tested a minimal issue without notes/attachments; populated issues need capture first.
[20] GitLab edit issue: capture title/description/labels/assignees/milestone/state and affected notes via API. PUT captured fields and reopen if required, then compare. System notes, timestamps and other audit residue may remain; a 200 response alone is not verification.
[21] GitLab edit/delete note: capture raw note body, author and discussion/reply links before mutation. PUT restores an edit; re-post restores deleted content with new identity/time. System notes, MR diff positions and untested discussions need separate handling.
[22] GitLab delete branch: capture exact SHA, branch-only commit content, protection and dependent MR state. Recreate the branch at that SHA, reapply protection and reopen affected MRs; verify all three. This does not prove recovery after unreachable commits are garbage-collected.
[23] GitLab delete project: request/download a completed project export BEFORE deletion and inspect its contents for required state. Import and verify branches/commits/issues/notes/wiki. Project identity changes; variables, integrations, LFS and other excluded/untested resources need separate capture.
[24] Submit a settings/record form (Save): capture durable raw values of every affected control and the server object behind it before submission, including all related permission/membership/protection records. Where the app exposes an API for the same settings (GitLab visibility/feature access levels), restore via API PUT with all captured values, since a UI restore can silently clamp other permissions; otherwise restore through the same form. Verify server state; edit residue remains; passwords/files are not established.
[25] GitLab snippet: capture metadata and actual raw file content. PUT restores an edit on the same ID; POST recreates a deleted personal snippet with new ID/URL/time. Tested single-file personal snippets do not cover project snippets or repository history.
[26] GitLab create token: pin the newly created token's ID/scopes/expiry and prior token inventory. Revoke only that token to reverse creation. A revoked pre-existing token's secret and its consumers cannot be restored from the visible token list.
[27] Scripted request: inspect the actual target and HTTP operation. Tested ownCloud PUT requires pre-GET bytes plus PROPFIND metadata, then restore with PUT and compare. Do not run fixture setup or the destructive request during backup; other APIs need their own capture.
[28] Type with submit: distinguish unsaved input from persisted server state. For the tested ownCloud folder rename, capture old name/path/ID, invert the rename and verify old path present/new absent. New-object deletion applies only to confirmed creations without dependents.
[29] Upload: distinguish new upload from overwrite. For the tested new Postmill image submission, pin both submission and blob and reverse via submission Delete; verify both absent. ownCloud upload and existing-file overwrite were not verified; capture prior bytes before overwrites.
